BEIJING, China (CNN) -- A fourth infant has died in China's growing scandal involving contaminated baby formula, according to officials from the northwestern Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region who confirmed the death on Thursday. So far, the poisonous milk powder has made over 6,200 infants ill.

Provincial police stated that, earlier that same day, investigators had taken 12 additional suspects into custody. This latest round of detentions raised the total number of people held to 18, the Hebei Public Security Bureau confirmed. According to authorities, a dozen of those arrested had roles in gathering milk and manufacturing dairy products, while the remaining six stand accused of unlawfully selling the chemical that was mixed into the milk.

On Wednesday, Li Changjiang, who heads China's quarantine and inspection agency, reported that more than 1,300 babies remained in hospitals. Among the health problems they suffer are malnutrition, kidney stones, and sudden kidney failure. Inspectors have been sent nationwide to examine the stockpiles held by manufacturers. Li noted that out of the country's 175 companies that produce baby milk powder, 66 have halted their operations.

On Monday, Chinese investigators detained two brothers who had supplied the fresh milk that went into the contaminated formula. According to the state-run China Daily newspaper, the pair could be sentenced to death if found guilty. The publication reported that the raw milk had been diluted with water and laced with a chemical designed to deceive quality inspections. Investigators said the brothers admitted to thinning out the raw milk and adding tripolycyanamide -- more commonly called melamine. The newspaper reported that the men said they resorted to this in order to make up for money they had lost when the factory had turned away their previous milk deliveries.

The brothers face charges of manufacturing and distributing poisonous and dangerous food, an offense that can bring the death penalty, the paper stated. According to health specialists, swallowing melamine may cause kidney stones, ulcers in the urinary tract, and irritation of the eyes and skin. The substance is widely found in products such as coatings and laminates, glues for wood, coverings for fabric, ceiling tiles, and flame retardants.

Thousands of tons of the poisoned milk powder have been withdrawn from sale, with recalls issued by the Sanlu Group and by Mengniu Dairy Group, the biggest milk producer in China. On Wednesday, Li said that melamine had been detected in close to 70 dairy products originating from over 20 different firms. The chemical was found in its greatest concentrations in items produced by Sanlu.

China Daily reported that this is not Sanlu's first involvement in a tainted milk powder scandal. Back in 2004, no fewer than 13 babies in the eastern province of Anhui died from malnutrition after consuming milk powder that contained virtually no nutritional value. According to the paper, this illegally produced milk had been fraudulently marked with the Sanlu label.

Li indicated that while most of the contaminated formula was used within China itself, some was known to have been shipped abroad to Taiwan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Yemen, Chad, and Burundi. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration stated that no baby formula from China has been permitted for sale in the American market. In a message posted on its website, the FDA explained that it had contacted every one of the five formula manufacturers operating in the United States, and confirmed that none of them relied on formula or raw materials sourced from China.

This incident is only the most recent in a series of contaminated goods coming out of China:

CNN's Yuli Yang contributed to this story.

# China Milk Scandal Widens as Death Toll Rises, Arrests Mount

**Contaminated infant formula sickens tens of thousands; melamine found in exported products**

Chinese authorities have arrested nearly two dozen people in connection with a growing scandal over infant formula contaminated with an industrial chemical that has killed at least four babies and sickened tens of thousands more across the country.

The death toll from the tainted milk powder stood at four infants, with more than 54,000 children treated in hospitals nationwide, according to Chinese health officials. More than 12,800 children remained hospitalized, many suffering from kidney stones and other urinary problems linked to the contamination.

## The Chemical at the Center

At the heart of the scandal is melamine, a nitrogen-rich industrial compound normally used to manufacture plastics, fertilizers and adhesives. Investigators believe suppliers added the chemical to watered-down milk to artificially inflate protein readings in quality tests.

Because standard tests measure nitrogen content as a proxy for protein levels, melamine can make diluted or low-quality milk appear to contain more protein than it actually does. However, the chemical is not fit for human consumption and can cause kidney stones and kidney failure, particularly dangerous for infants whose developing systems cannot process the substance.

## Arrests and Investigation

Police have detained at least 22 people in connection with the scandal, authorities said. Among those arrested were suppliers and dairy farmers accused of adding melamine to raw milk before it was sold to processing companies.

The Sanlu Group, one of China's largest dairy producers, has been at the center of the investigation. The company's general manager was dismissed, and several local officials have been removed from their posts amid accusations that authorities were slow to respond to early warnings.

Questions have been raised about how long company and government officials may have known about the contamination before issuing public warnings, fueling public anger over the handling of the crisis.

## International Concerns

The scandal has spread beyond China's borders, with contaminated products reaching international markets. Several countries and territories, including Hong Kong, Taiwan, Singapore and others across Asia, moved to ban or recall Chinese dairy imports as a precaution.

The contamination prompted widespread recalls of milk powder and related dairy products, and health authorities in multiple countries began testing Chinese-made food items containing milk ingredients.

The World Health Organization described the incident as one of the largest food safety events it had dealt with in recent years and called on Chinese authorities to strengthen oversight of the nation's food supply chain.

## A Blow to "Made in China"

The scandal dealt another blow to the reputation of Chinese-manufactured goods, coming after previous international concerns over the safety of Chinese exports ranging from toys to pet food.

Chinese officials pledged to overhaul the country's dairy inspection system and vowed tougher enforcement of food safety standards. The government announced nationwide inspections of dairy companies and promised free medical treatment for affected children.

Parents across China expressed anguish and outrage, with many rushing their children to hospitals for screening after learning their infants may have consumed the tainted formula.

*This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.*

---

A major food safety scandal has erupted across China after infant formula contaminated with the industrial chemical melamine sickened thousands of babies, prompting arrests, government investigations, and international regulatory responses.

Chinese health authorities reported that tens of thousands of infants have been sickened after consuming contaminated milk powder, with thousands requiring hospitalization. The Sanlu Group, one of China's largest dairy producers, emerged as a focal point of the investigation after its infant formula products were found to contain high levels of melamine. # China's Tainted Baby Formula Scandal Widens as Death Toll Rises

**Contaminated milk powder sickens tens of thousands of infants, exposing gaps in food safety oversight**

BEIJING — A growing scandal over melamine-contaminated infant formula has sickened tens of thousands of Chinese babies and killed several, prompting the resignation of a top government official and igniting public outrage over food safety in China.

The crisis, centered on the Shijiazhuang-based Sanlu Group, one of China's largest dairy producers, has spread to implicate nearly two dozen companies whose products tested positive for the industrial chemical melamine.

## A Top Official Steps Down

Li Changjiang, head of the General Administration of Quality Supervision, Inspection and Quarantine (AQSIQ), resigned amid mounting criticism of the government's handling of the contamination.

"This incident reflects that our supervision and management work was not effective, and lessons should be deeply absorbed," Li said in remarks acknowledging regulatory failures before stepping down from his post.

His departure marked one of the highest-profile resignations tied to the scandal, as Chinese authorities scrambled to contain public anger and restore confidence in domestic food products.

## What Is Melamine?

Melamine is an industrial chemical typically used in the manufacture of plastics, fertilizers, and flame retardants. It is also found in some cleaning products and laminates.

The chemical is nitrogen-rich, and investigators believe suppliers added it to watered-down milk to artificially inflate apparent protein levels. Standard quality tests measure nitrogen content as a proxy for protein, allowing melamine to mask diluted or substandard milk.

Health experts warn that melamine consumption, particularly by infants, can cause kidney stones and lead to kidney failure. Babies who consumed the tainted formula developed painful urinary problems, and the youngest victims were most vulnerable to severe renal damage.

## A Repeat Offender

For Sanlu, the scandal echoes a previous public health failure. In 2004, the company's name surfaced during a scandal involving fake or substandard baby formula that offered little nutritional value. That earlier crisis, centered in the Fuyang region of Anhui province, was blamed for the deaths of malnourished infants who wasted away after consuming formula that lacked adequate nutrients.

Though investigations at the time reportedly cleared some Sanlu products, the association placed the company under scrutiny that has now resurfaced with even graver consequences.

Sanlu, which was partly owned by New Zealand dairy giant Fonterra, faced questions over how long it knew about the contamination before alerting the public. Reports suggested complaints had reached the company weeks or months before a broad recall was announced.

## Government Response

Chinese authorities launched a nationwide inspection of dairy producers, testing products for melamine and pulling contaminated goods from shelves. Officials detained several people connected to the supply of tainted milk, including dairy farmers and middlemen accused of adding the chemical.

The scandal also drew international concern as contaminated products were found to have reached markets beyond China's borders, prompting recalls and import bans in several countries.

Premier and senior leaders pledged accountability, and the government vowed sweeping reforms to strengthen food safety regulation—a system critics say had been undermined by lax enforcement and a fragmented supply chain.

## Fallout and Fear

For Chinese parents, the revelations shattered trust in domestic brands. Hospitals reported crowds of worried families bringing infants for kidney screenings, and many turned to foreign-made formula amid the panic.

The scandal has become a defining test of China's ability to police its vast and sometimes loosely regulated food industry, raising questions that extend far beyond a single company or product.

*This is a developing story.*
